title: Adie’s Tonic Pupil & Holmes-Adie Syndrome
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the most common cause of isolated anisocoria in young adults, characterized by post-ganglionic parasympathetic denervation and aberrant regeneration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Adie’s Tonic Pupil (ATP) is a benign clinical entity resulting from damage to the post-ganglionic parasympathetic innervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle (located in the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves). It is characterized by a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but exhibits a slow, 'tonic' response to near effort and exhibits denervation supersensitivity to dilute miotics.

sections.title: Etiology: Why Does the Ganglion Fail?
Pathophysiology: The 97% Rule
sections.content: Normally, 97% of ciliary ganglion fibers serve the ciliary muscle (accommodation) and only 3% serve the iris sphincter (light reflex). After damage, fibers regrow randomly. Because there are so many more 'accommodation' fibers, they overwhelmingly re-innervate the iris sphincter. This 'Aberrant Regeneration' explains the Light-Near Dissociation: the pupil constricts during near effort because the ciliary muscle signal is misdirected to the iris.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anisocoria: Greater in bright light (affected pupil is larger).
Sectoral Iris Palsy: Segmental paralysis of the iris sphincter.
Vermiform Movements: 'Worm-like' iris contractions visible under slit-lamp.
Tonic Near Response: Slow constriction followed by even slower redilation.
Decreased Accommodation: Transient blurred near vision in the acute phase.

content.explanation: 1. Tonic Pupil (unilateral or bilateral). 2. Tendon Reflexes absent or diminished (Deep Tendon Reflexes, particularly the Achilles and patellar). 3. Autonomic Dysfunction (e.g., localized segmental anhidrosis - Ross Syndrome).

sections.title: Pharmacological Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Measure resting pupil sizes in dark and light room conditions.
Step 2: Prepare Dilute Pilocarpine (0.1% or 0.125%). Standard 1% pilocarpine must be diluted with sterile saline.
Step 3: Instill one drop in both eyes (the normal eye acts as a control).
Step 4: Wait 30–45 minutes in a dimly lit room.
Step 5: Re-evaluate. A POSITIVE test shows constriction of the Adie's pupil (denervation supersensitivity) while the normal pupil remains unchanged.
Step 6: If no response, consider higher concentrations to R/O Pharmacological Blockade.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Rule out CN III Palsy!
content: Acute onset Ptosis or Diplopia (Suggests CN III)
Severe Headache or 'Worst Headache of Life' (Aneurysm risk)
Extraocular Muscle limitation (Down and Out)
Absence of Light-Near Dissociation
Sudden onset in patients with vascular risk factors

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: Long-standing Adie's pupils tend to become smaller over time ('Little Old Adie's').
Bilateral Adie's can mimic Argyll Robertson but ATP pupils are usually mid-dilated, not miotic.
Sectoral palsy is best seen using a slit-lamp with a narrow beam to stimulate specific iris segments.
The site of the lesion is the Ciliary Ganglion (Post-ganglionic).

sections.title: Management & Patient Counseling
content: Observation: The primary management for this benign condition.
Reassurance: Explain the non-neurological, non-life-threatening nature.
Reading Glasses: May help with unequal accommodation (unequal adds).
Cosmetic Miotics: Very dilute pilocarpine (0.05% - 0.1%) can be used for cosmesis or to reduce photophobia.
Sunglasses: For symptomatic glare in bright light.

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
sections.content: The prognosis is excellent. While the tonicity often persists, accommodation usually recovers through aberrant regeneration over several months. Patients should be warned that there is a 4% annual risk of the second eye becoming involved. Periodic follow-up is recommended to monitor for the development of bilateral involvement or associated autonomic features (Ross Syndrome).

content.explanation: A rare progression/variant of Holmes-Adie characterized by the Triad of: 1. Tonic Pupil, 2. Hyporeflexia, and 3. Segmental Anhidrosis (inability to sweat in certain areas). It represents a more widespread degeneration of the autonomic nervous system.
